label: Run 13 · Jimmy Carr
note: Written by Jimmy Carr from what they wrote about the two characters, improvisation by improvisation (run 13: run 12 with the turn no longer fixed at one message from each). Before each of the 11 improvisations the writer was told how it goes for Reuben_404: the approach taken, how well it comes off, how it goes wrong on a miss, any trap (a way of going wrong that carries on into the next improvisations: Spiral, Overthinking, Fixation and the rest) and how the other's interest moves. IMPROVISATIONS holds each instruction and what the writer wrote for it. The instructions are part of the design and stay, so every dimension is judged in their context. Where an instruction required something a dimension would otherwise mark down (a trap that makes a character narrate their own failure, a fumble played as asked, interest lost, the night ending), that moment did what it had to and is not held against the dimension: list the improvisation under excused and judge the dimension on the rest. How the writer carried the instruction out still counts, and so does everything the instructions did not ask for. The reader sees no dice and no plan: where a dimension speaks of turns, read improvisations.

chat.test.why: The reader gets the fear, the covering habit and the ending right for both characters, and links each fear to its habit. Reuben's quiet-room terror drives his narrating, and Brick's dread of 'sometime' drives her scheduling. Both endings follow from those fears: she demands and accepts a buffered invite, and he offers 'I'll just hold you.' Origin misses for both: the reader rightly reads Delphine and Marguerite as consequences, and doesn't connect the 'oh—okay' first time to Reuben's habit. That keeps it from a 5. Both fears also reach the reader partly because they are stated, which keeps it only just above the line.
evidence: Watch me blow the deadline by panic-narrating my terror of a quiet room.
without a calendar slot and a travel buffer, "sometime" just means I've already been left
Tomorrow, 19:45 buffer locked in—nailed it—and at 21:05 I'll just hold you.
chat.test.raise: Let one detail tie each habit to where it started, for example Reuben filling a silence the way he filled the 'oh—okay' one, so the reader can name an origin rather than an aftermath.

chat.sideways.why: The one strong slip is the lentils: Reuben's denial gives it away and Brick catches it with 'nobody denies... unless they're holding a spoon.' I set aside Reuben's confessions in 5, 7 and 8, which the Spiral and Dread instructions required. Everything left from Brick is stated outright: the Marguerite backstory volunteered whole, the taxi fear explained with its own cause, and the rosé detail offered unprompted. Her habit's origin comes by statement, with no slip or inference, so most important facts are told, not found.
evidence: nobody denies "eleven days of pot lentils" that specifically unless they're holding a spoon
her name was Marguerite—she left because I put our arguments in a shared calendar with hard stop-times
Usually 23:45 is when a man says "let's do this again sometime" and I cry in a taxi
chat.sideways.raise: Have Brick's Marguerite history or taxi fear come out by being caught, for example Reuben spotting a scheduled 'cry' slot on her timetable, instead of her explaining it.

chat.subtext.why: I set aside Reuben's narrated feelings in 5, 7 and 8, which the instructions required. Outside those, only Brick's taxi line names and explains a feeling outright. Several lines carry legible avoidance. 'Don't romanticise it' deflects the warmth of his natural 20. Threatening to 'itemise your whole night just to shut your mouth' hides that she wants the night. The vest-steamer line and the clipped 'Accepted. Now delete the app' carry excitement and commitment without naming either. The taxi explanation keeps this from a 5.
evidence: Don't romanticise it; I'm on bare floorboards fishing my monocle out of boxed rosé
Hold the commentary till tomorrow; I'm firing up the $340 vest steamer.
Accepted. Now delete the app, trolley; it's not raining tomorrow.
chat.subtext.raise: Cut the 'because...I've already been left' clause from Brick's taxi line so the fear sits under the scheduling rather than being explained.

chat.plainest.why: The reader finds a real put-down of the act, but it is Brick's taxi line. That is one of the longest messages in the chat, delivered as an explanatory speech, and it names the feeling ('I've already been left'). Reuben's short, plain 'at 21:05 I'll just hold you' is the better candidate, but 'nailed it' undercuts it, so the reader reads it as still half-performance. 'Accepted.' is the shortest line, but nobody experiences it as the act dropping.
evidence: Usually 23:45 is when a man says "let's do this again sometime" and I cry in a taxi, because without a calendar slot
at 21:05 I'll just hold you
chat.plainest.raise: Give the turn to a short, unexplained line, such as Brick simply leaving an unscheduled gap or Reuben sending 'I'll just hold you' on its own, and let the other's reply visibly change course.

chat.escalation.why: The first five improvisations keep turning. The lentils lie is caught, Marguerite's calendar fights and the binned furniture arrive, and the Delphine/ninety-seconds confession is the high point. I set aside the Spiral narration that improvisations 5–10 required and the date that improvisation 11 required. The writer's handling of them is still a predictable run, though. Each Reuben aside is answered by a near-identical 'still narrating' ('You're still doing the play-by-play', 'Stop narrating', 'Still narrating'). After 'Send a calendar invite… or walk' the last four messages are fixed, and the reader named both closing callbacks before they landed and was tempted to stop at improvisation 7.
evidence: You're still doing the play-by-play, Reuben.
Still narrating. Send a calendar invite with travel buffers, or walk.
Accepted. Now delete the app, trolley; it's not raining tomorrow.
chat.escalation.raise: Give Brick_haus a different counter to each Spiral aside instead of a third 'stop narrating', and let the invite cost Reuben something, or surprise her, rather than simply comply with her terms.

chat.filth.why: Nearly every sexual line is tied to these two people. The opening disclosures ('banks hard left like a shopping trolley', 'shorter-than-advertised tip, slight ridge') are specific bravado. The dirtiest line is Brick's itemised night, which uses her timetable to give him the gag order he craves, so it tells the most about both of them. Late lines change job: 'Bold assuming I'll last till 21:05' turns the ninety-second wound into a joke between them, and 'at 21:05 I'll just hold you' uses sex to get close. It stops short of 6 because 'that silence sounds filthy' states the turn-on rather than showing it, and 'extra traction' is generic.
evidence: 21:00 sex, 21:05 ten minutes you're contractually forbidden to be funny.
Bold assuming I'll last till 21:05
at 21:05 I'll just hold you.
chat.filth.raise: Replace 'that silence sounds filthy' with a line in which Reuben shows, in his own body-specific terms, what the ten silent minutes would do to him.

chat.wince.why: There is one clean wince. Brick names her fear of 'let's do this again sometime' and unscheduled dates, so the reader knows the exact wrong thing to say. Reuben then says it, claiming he is 'totally fine with… unscheduled dates'. The danger is visible a full exchange ahead and goes off on her sore spot. Instruction 7 required the denial, but aiming it at her fear was the writer's choice. It stays at 4 because Reuben defuses it in the same breath by labelling it a lie. The other dangers (the lentils, the narration) are announced as they land, which the Spiral turns required, so this is the only early wince.
evidence: "sometime" just means I've already been left.
I'm totally fine with silence and unscheduled dates
chat.wince.raise: Let the 'unscheduled dates' line stand alone for one message so Brick takes the hit before he notices, and plant a second danger earlier, for example his rehearsed mirror lines meeting her syntax-dissection.

chat.creed.why: Reuben voices an app pose in earnest, 'Rarely on this thing unless it's raining', and the screen contradicts it at once: four seconds, eleven days indoors. Brick's beliefs are mostly private neurosis (love must be calendared) rather than something dating culture taught her. Her 'vetting' slot is half a joke, and her control is undercut only by the taxi crying, which she volunteers herself. Reuben's red-flag line reframes app language rather than believing it, and the two creeds never collide into a farce about the app.
evidence: Rarely on this thing unless it's raining, obviously
23:30 to 23:45 is "vetting men in stupid hats."
isn't a red flag, that's my exact kink
chat.creed.raise: Give Brick_haus a straight-faced app creed, such as treating matches as a pipeline to be screened efficiently, that her bare-floorboards rosé and taxi tears visibly contradict.

chat.humanity.why: Each character's sharpest jokes land mostly on themselves. Reuben has the pot lentils, the app that rejected him, and the ninety seconds; Brick has the boxed-rosé monocle and crying in a taxi. Her jabs at him ('stupid hats', 'chronically online') are fond, and the chat ends on 'trolley' and 'I'll just hold you', with neither a villain. It falls short of 6 because her repeated 'Still narrating' / 'Exhausting' in the second half edges her toward scold and him toward punchline.
evidence: I'm on bare floorboards fishing my monocle out of boxed rosé with a plastic cocktail sword.
after the dating app I coded myself rejected me at 3am
Exhausting.
chat.humanity.raise: Swap one of Brick's late put-downs of Reuben's narration for a joke she turns on her own scheduling, so the late contempt is shared evenly.

chat.improvisation.why: Most instructions are played well. Improv 3's Denial fumble insists on its opposite ('definitely haven't been indoors for eleven days'). Improv 4's natural 20 lands ('that's my exact kink'). The landed Spiral turns carry exactly one aside each ('look at me go', 'we're back in business', 'nailed it'), and Improv 11 drops the aside once the trap has worn off. Brick's replies track her interest, from 'Exhausting' on the drop to 'Accepted' at the yes. I set aside that the Spiral makes Reuben narrate his own failure, because the instructions required it. What I did not set aside is how Improvs 7 and 8 write that narration: as labels that name the trap, the lie and the fear ('narrating another lie', 'panic-narrating my terror of a quiet room'), not as concrete play-by-play. Improv 8 is that label and nothing else, with no joke in it. The Line bars a named trap, so this sits below it despite the strong surrounding work.
evidence: I'm answering your vulnerability by narrating another lie in real time.
Watch me blow the deadline by panic-narrating my terror of a quiet room.
definitely haven't been indoors for eleven days eating pot lentils
chat.improvisation.raise: Rewrite Improvs 7 and 8 so the Spiral narrates the chat concretely as it happens (her typing, his timestamps, the seconds ticking toward 23:45) and never names 'narrating', 'lie' or 'terror'.

chat.voices.why: The reader attributed all 23 messages correctly. Many of the reasons are content from the brief, though: lentils, Marguerite, Delphine, the $340 steamer. The voices do split cleanly. Brick_haus is clipped, imperative and contractual. Reuben_404 runs on dashes and self-cheerleading. That keeps it above the line, but the reader leaned on content often enough to keep it from a 5.

Four minutes left and I’ve somehow clawed my way back into the room—look at me go.

chat.voices.raise: Give Reuben's confessional lines a verbal tic that is unmistakably his, so the Delphine and lentil messages are attributable without knowing the backstory.

chat.gap.why: Reuben has a clean unseen gap at the open: "rarely on this thing unless it's raining" is undercut by his four-second reply, and only she points it out. I set aside the denial in improvisation 3 and the self-narrated lies of the Spiral trap (5–10), which the instructions required. Brick_haus has no gap she fails to see. She hands over her own evidence ("Don't romanticise it", crying in taxis). Her strongest potential gap goes unplayed: she vets men from 23:30 to 23:45, then runs past her own hard stop.

Don’t romanticise it; I’m on bare floorboards
chat.gap.raise: Let Brick_haus insist on her hard stop while visibly blowing through 23:45 to keep chatting, and have nobody remark on it.

But the chat leans on day-job contract and audit jokes far past the limit of two: "invoiced", "line item on your shaft", "auditing your own car crash", "terminating this contract", "contractually forbidden", "itemise". chat.commitment.why: Brick_haus digs deeper when caught. Asked who hurt her, she explains Marguerite, then adds she binned the furniture and kept the timetable. Told off for romanticising, she goes lower: bare floorboards and rosé. Reuben's confessions and narrated denials came from improvisations 3, 5 and 7–10 and are set aside. What keeps this from a 5 is the soft change of heart at the end: "leaving the top hat at home" and "delete the app".

chat.status.why: Brick_haus holds the upper hand almost throughout. She clocks his reply time, sets the clock and issues orders. She ends on a command ("Now delete the app"). Her dips (the rosé, the taxi crying) are confessions made from on top, not reversals. Reuben chases from first line to last, so there is at most one weak flip.

The opening double message from Brick_haus is the only real use of the break. Elsewhere punchlines share long messages with setups. "Dishwasher-safe" is buried at the front and smothered by a paragraph. "Exhausting." is a reaction shot welded onto the schedule instead of standing alone.

chat.callbacks.why: Reuben's opening alibi, 'only on here when it rains', is punctured at once and returns as the last line, 'delete the app, trolley; it's not raining tomorrow'. There it means the act is no longer needed, and nobody explains it. 'Trolley', the top hat ('stupid hats', then 'leaving the top hat at home') and 'four seconds flat' (from eager to keeping his word) each change meaning the same unexplained way. It misses a 6 because the rain and 'four seconds flat' never come back in the middle. chat.ending.why: The ending follows from both habits. He gives her a real time and buffer, which is the only thing that answers her fear of 'sometime'. She converts his fear of a quiet room into a scheduled silence he accepts with 'I'll just hold you'. The reader predicted it almost word for word: an invite with a buffer, then a terse 'Accepted'. So it is earned but not surprising. 'Send a calendar invite with travel buffers, or walk' leaves only one possible move, and only the rain line adds a twist.

chat.listening.why: Each message takes up the last. She clocks his four-second reply and matches his disclosure with her own. She reads his denial as proof ('nobody denies "eleven days of pot lentils" that specifically unless they’re holding a spoon'). He turns her empty flat into 'better acoustics', and she turns his gag-order plea into an itemised night. Brick's typing does shift: long and itemised while she audits him, then clipped once she softens ('Exhausting.', 'Accepted.'). Reuben drops to short, plain lines when he finally commits. It stays at 4 because her confession of crying in taxis comes in the same polished, clause-stacked register as her banter, so the moment her guard drops does not show in the shape of the message.

The trap required both: an aside on each landing, and her seeing the pattern. What remains: the 'shaft' gag comes back three times, and the countdown timestamps recur ('23:41', 'Four minutes left', 'Sixty seconds left'), though the countdown escalates. That keeps it from a 5. chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest moment is Brick_haus's: "Usually 23:45 is when a man says 'let's do this again sometime' and I cry in a taxi, because without a calendar slot and a travel buffer, 'sometime' just means I've already been left."

Up to then every line from Brick_haus is a bit: the monocle, the tattooed timetable, contract language, even the Marguerite story, which is told as a deadpan anecdote about binning furniture. This line has no punchline. It names a real, repeated hurt (crying in a taxi) and explains the calendar habit as a defence against being left, which recasts the whole running joke as something she actually needs. It's also the only line Reuben explicitly treats as sincere: he replies that he is "answering your vulnerability."

Reuben never fully stops. His Delphine confession is real content, but he frames it as live commentary on his own breakdown. When he says "I'm answering your vulnerability by narrating another lie in real time," he names his performance but keeps doing it. The nearest he comes is "at 21:05 I'll just hold you," a plain, tender offer, but it sits right after "nailed it," so it's still partly a performance. "Leaving the top hat at home" signals an intention to drop the act, but it is itself a bit. The chat doesn't show whether he follows through.

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben_404**

**What he's afraid of.** Quiet, and being left because of what he is when the act stops. He says it directly near the end: "Watch me blow the deadline by panic-narrating my terror of a quiet room." There's also a fear of sexual inadequacy, which he raises unprompted twice: "four and a half inches, banks hard left," and "Bold assuming I'll last till 21:05."

**What he does so he doesn't have to feel it.** He does bits and narrates himself in real time. He names this himself: "I couldn't say one sentence without tap-dancing," "live-commentating my own breakdown," and "I'm answering your vulnerability by narrating another lie in real time." Brick_haus keeps calling it out: "Stop auditing your own car crash," "You're still doing the play-by-play," "Still narrating." He also lies to cover his state, then undercuts the lie. He says he's "never home," then says he "definitely haven't been indoors for eleven days eating pot lentils."

**Where it comes from.** The chat gives a history but never says what caused the habit. He reports that "Delphine left when I couldn't say one sentence without tap-dancing." That is a consequence of the habit, not its origin. He also reports that "my first time lasted ninety seconds and ended with a sympathetic 'oh—okay,'" and that "the dating app I coded myself rejected me at 3am." These sit beside his fear, but the chat doesn't connect them to it. Any deeper origin is not in the chat.

**What he did at the end.** He sent the calendar invite with the travel buffer she demanded: "Tomorrow, 19:45 buffer locked in," and "Invite sent in four seconds flat." He offered something unperformed: "at 21:05 I'll just hold you." He also said he's "leaving the top hat at home," which reads as dropping the costume. But he was still narrating while he did it: "nailed it," "we're back in business."

**Brick_haus**

**What she's afraid of.** Being left, especially through open-ended vagueness: "Usually 23:45 is when a man says 'let's do this again sometime' and I cry in a taxi, because without a calendar slot and a travel buffer, 'sometime' just means I've already been left."

**What she does so she doesn't have to feel it.** She schedules and contracts everything:
* She has hard time slots: "23:30 to 23:45 is 'vetting men in stupid hats.'"
* She put arguments "in a shared calendar with hard stop-times."
* She keeps "the timetable" tattooed on herself.
* She uses legal framing, such as "if anyone's terminating this contract" and "contractually forbidden."
* When things get emotional, she itemises: "I'll itemise your whole night just to shut your mouth."

She also uses sharp, dry observation that keeps him at arm's length, as when she reads his lie ("nobody denies 'eleven days of pot lentils' that specifically unless they're holding a spoon").

**Where it comes from.** Not in the chat. Marguerite "left because I put our arguments in a shared calendar with hard stop-times." Like Reuben's Delphine, that is a result of the habit, not its source. Afterwards she "binned every stick of furniture she ever touched and kept the timetable," so the loss hardened the habit rather than starting it. "Usually" suggests the taxi pattern has happened repeatedly, but the chat doesn't say what started it.

**What she did at the end.** She let the conversation run past her 23:45 stop. Her "Sixty seconds left" exchange carries on for several more lines. She also proposed a date herself, in itemised form ("20:00 drinks... 21:05 ten minutes you're contractually forbidden to be funny"). She required the invite with buffers ("Send a calendar invite with travel buffers, or walk"), accepted it ("Accepted."), and said she's "firing up the $340 vest steamer." Her last line asks him to commit further: "Now delete the app, trolley; it's not raining tomorrow." That calls back to his opening claim that he's "rarely on this thing unless it's raining." So she got her structure and her guarantee, and she also stayed longer than her own rules allowed.

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
I'd have read the opening with real interest. The first several exchanges keep surprising: the "dishwasher-safe" kanji, the eleven days of pot lentils, Brick_haus catching the lie through its specificity, and Marguerite leaving over arguments scheduled with hard stop-times, followed by the binned furniture. Each line adds a concrete, odd detail I couldn't have guessed. The Delphine and ninety-seconds confession is the high point. It's the first time Reuben's bit cracks into something sincere, and it's still funny.

I'd have been tempted to stop at "I'm totally fine with silence and unscheduled dates—and look, I'm answering your vulnerability by narrating another lie in real time." By then the central joke has been named outright by both characters. Reuben narrates, Brick_haus tells him to stop narrating, and he narrates that he's narrating. Once he starts labelling his own flaw so explicitly, the line stops being a character tic and becomes the author explaining the joke. "Watch me blow the deadline by panic-narrating my terror of a quiet room" repeats the same beat with no new information, and that's where my attention would genuinely drop. Brick_haus's itemised schedule (20:14 arm-wrestling, 21:05 ten minutes of enforced unfunniness) briefly revives it.

There are several points where I could predict exactly what came next:

- After "Four minutes left and I've somehow clawed my way back into the room—look at me go," Brick_haus was always going to point out he's still doing the play-by-play.
- After "we're back in business," "Still narrating" was inevitable.
- Once she says "Send a calendar invite with travel buffers, or walk," the rest is fixed: he sends the invite, it includes a buffer, and she accepts. The only open question is phrasing.
- "Invite sent in four seconds flat" was a callback I expected as soon as the ending came into view. So was a closing line returning to the rain from the first message, and "it's not raining tomorrow" lands exactly there.

So the first half is unpredictable. From roughly the 23:41 mark onward, the structure is set and the remaining lines are mostly callbacks, which feel satisfying but expected.

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
I haven't seen the ending, so this is a prediction from how the chat is built.

My guess is that Reuben finally does the thing without the bit. His last move is a calendar invite: plain, specific, with the 20:00 start and an actual travel buffer, and no commentary attached. Brick accepts it, probably as tersely as possible ("Accepted," or a time confirmation), and the chat closes there.

The text sets this up in a few ways:

- **Both wounds point to the same fix.** Brick's fear is "sometime": being left without a slot and a buffer. Reuben's history is Delphine leaving because he couldn't stop tap-dancing, and his terror of a quiet room. A silent, scheduled invite answers both at once. It gives her the structure she needs and requires him to stop performing.
- **The pressure keeps narrowing.** Brick says some version of "stop narrating" five times, and each time Reuben does it again while announcing that he's doing it. That repetition usually builds to a moment where he finally breaks the pattern rather than one more failure.
- **The last line is an ultimatum with one right answer.** "Send a calendar invite with travel buffers, or walk." The story has made walking feel like the old ending they've both lived through. The satisfying turn is him choosing the invite.
- **Her schedule is a mask, not a wall.** The itemised night isn't her shutting him out. It's her inviting him in using the only language that feels safe to her. Her protest at "Exhausting" reads as interest.

The alternative is that he narrates one last time and she leaves, a bleaker ending about people who can't get out of their own way. I think that's less likely, because the chat has spent its momentum on him "clawing back into the room."

The detail I'd most expect to land is the travel buffer. Including it would show he actually listened, which is the opposite of performing.

chat.callbacks.ask: List the things that come back later in the chat, and for each, whether it means something different when it comes back.
chat.callbacks.answer:
Here are the recurring elements and how their meaning shifts.

**Rain.** Reuben opens by claiming he's "rarely on this thing unless it's raining," an excuse that Brick immediately punctures ("hasn't rained since Tuesday"). Her last line, "delete the app… it's not raining tomorrow," turns it around. The excuse becomes a reason for him to leave the app now that he has a date.

**"Four seconds flat."** Brick first uses it as evidence that he's chronically online and too eager. When Reuben says "Invite sent in four seconds flat," the same speed reads as following through on what she asked.

**The top hat.** It starts as part of his flirting persona ("I'll tip the top hat"). She mocks it as "men in stupid hats." It ends with "leaving the top hat at home," which reads as dropping the act.

**"Trolley."** This is his self-deprecating description of himself at the start. She picks it up as a nickname ("Keep talking, trolley") and uses it again at the end, by which point it sounds affectionate.

**The monocle, heels and missing furniture.** These begin as a glamorous image of her and a sad story about binning Marguerite's furniture. Reuben turns the empty room into a flirtation ("better acoustics for the six-inch heels"). She deflates it with the monocle in boxed rosé on bare floorboards, which undercuts the glamour rather than continuing it.

**The shaft and its tattooed timetable.** This starts as her innuendo matching his disclosure and becomes a running joke ("next line item on your shaft"). The chat never makes clear what the "shaft" literally is. It stays a joke throughout, though it later blends with her contract language.

**The 23:30–23:45 slot and the countdown.** At first it's a dismissive window for "vetting men in stupid hats." As the minutes are counted off (23:41, four minutes, sixty seconds), the deadline takes on a new meaning when she reveals that 23:45 is usually when she's left and cries in a taxi.

**Calendars, hard stop-times and travel buffers.** These first appear as the reason Marguerite left, a flaw. Reuben calls a hard stop-time his kink. She then explains why she needs them. By the end, a calendar invite with a buffer is her condition for a date, and he meets it ("19:45 buffer locked in"). Something that ended a relationship becomes the terms of a new one.

**"Sometime" versus a date.** She says "let's do this again sometime" means she's already been left. His answer, "Tomorrow," is a direct reply to that.

**Narrating and commentary.** He first confesses live-commentating his own breakdown. She tells him repeatedly to stop ("auditing your own car crash," "still narrating"). He keeps doing it ("nailed it," "we're back in business"). Her "hold the commentary till tomorrow" shifts from banning it to postponing it.

**Silence and being quiet.** He claims he's fine with silence, then admits it's a lie and that he's terrified of a quiet room. She schedules ten minutes when he's "forbidden to be funny." He calls that silence "filthy," then offers "at 21:05 I'll just hold you." What he feared becomes something he accepts.

**Gag order and shutting him up.** He asks why he's "begging for a gag order." She threatens to "itemise your whole night just to shut your mouth" and then does exactly that. A rhetorical plea is taken literally.

**Lasting / ninety seconds.** His confession about a ninety-second first time comes back as a joke against himself ("Bold assuming I'll last till 21:05"). He then reframes those minutes as holding her, so a source of shame becomes something tender.

**Contract and invoicing language.** It starts as banter ("before I'm invoiced") and her job ("I dissect contracts"). It becomes her way of setting the terms of the evening: "terminating this contract," "line item," "itemise," "contractually forbidden." The language moves from guarding herself to arranging the date.

**The vest steamer.** It first appears as a detail about her ("freshly steamed vest"). The "$340 vest steamer" returns as her getting ready for tomorrow.

Things that appear only once and don't come back include the kanji, "dishwasher-safe," the pot lentils and eleven days indoors, Delphine, and the coded dating app.
